steps.title: The words that tell you where the argument is going
steps.sub: Read this before the texts. You will use it immediately.
steps.html:
A linker is a signpost. It tells you, before you read the sentence, what that sentence is going to do to the one before it.

Adding: moreover, in addition, furthermore, what is more. Contrasting: however, nevertheless, on the other hand, although, whereas. Result: therefore, so, as a result, consequently. Restating: in other words, that is to say. Example: for example, for instance, such as.

The most useful ones for reading are the contrast linkers, because they mark the turn in an argument. When you see However, Nevertheless, or Although, the writer is about to take something back or push against what they just said.

Nevertheless is worth knowing precisely: it means despite that, this is still true. It concedes and then refuses to give way.

Practical technique: when you skim a text, read the linkers and the sentence that follows each one. That is usually where the argument lives.

steps.title: Text A · One afternoon in Amsterdam
steps.html:
Written for this course, from the Repair Café International Foundation’s published account of its own history.

The idea did not come up in a laboratory. In 2009 a Dutch journalist called Martine Postma, who had been writing about sustainability and had noticed how much her neighbours were throwing away, came up with something specific: one afternoon, one hall, free coffee, and volunteers who could hold a screwdriver. The first Repair Café was held in Amsterdam on 18 October 2009. She was not sure anybody would turn up. Instead, people arrived early, carrying appliances, clothes, furniture and, in at least one case, a musical instrument.

What happened next was not planned either. So many groups wanted to do the same thing that a foundation was set up in March 2010 simply to answer them, and it began producing manuals, posters and a starter kit so that nobody had to work out the format from scratch. Consequently, similar shops popped up in one country after another. By 2016 there were more than a thousand registered; today the figure has passed three thousand. Admittedly, that is still small against the scale of what gets discarded — but it grew without advertising, which is unusual.

The foundation has also tried to sort out a problem the volunteers created themselves. Every session generates knowledge — which brands fail, which faults recur, which parts cannot be bought — and for years all of it stayed in people’s heads. In 2017, therefore, an online tool was launched so that groups could record what each repair turned out to involve. Moreover, the records made it possible to compare one town with another. In other words, a movement built on Saturday afternoons quietly began to carry out research.

steps.title: Text B · What a Saturday actually looks like
steps.html:
Written for this course. The town described here is a composite of several such groups.

In practice, a session looks less impressive than the numbers. In one English town that started a group after a public meeting, nineteen people turned up on the first Saturday, most of them over sixty, and they repaired forty-one things before lunch. Nobody had to make up a reason for coming. A lamp is not a symbol of anything; it is a lamp, and it either works afterwards or it does not.

The economics are what persuade councils, however, rather than the sentiment. A repair typically costs a fraction of a replacement, and volunteers find out very quickly that a surprising share of dead appliances have one cheap broken part. Nevertheless, nobody pretends the saving is large in itself. Therefore the case for the shop tends to be financial before it is ever environmental. In that town the funding ran out in the second winter, and yet the group stayed open, staffed by eleven volunteers and one paid hour a week.

None of which has fixed the underlying problem. Manufacturers still design products that are difficult to open, and several countries are only now beginning to phase out the rules that allowed it. Even so, the interesting part of the story is not the tools or the money. What turned out to matter was that somebody organised an afternoon and other people came. That is the least repeatable part of it, and it is the only part the starter kit cannot explain, which is presumably why the foundation spends so much of its time answering the same question from towns that already have everything else they need.

Text A · One afternoon in Amsterdam

Written for this course, from the Repair Café International Foundation’s published account of its own history.

The idea did not come up in a laboratory. In 2009 a Dutch journalist called Martine Postma, who had been writing about sustainability and had noticed how much her neighbours were throwing away, came up with something specific: one afternoon, one hall, free coffee, and volunteers who could hold a screwdriver. The first Repair Café was held in Amsterdam on 18 October 2009. She was not sure anybody would turn up. Instead, people arrived early, carrying appliances, clothes, furniture and, in at least one case, a musical instrument.

What happened next was not planned either. So many groups wanted to do the same thing that a foundation was set up in March 2010 simply to answer them, and it began producing manuals, posters and a starter kit so that nobody had to work out the format from scratch. Consequently, similar shops popped up in one country after another. By 2016 there were more than a thousand registered; today the figure has passed three thousand. Admittedly, that is still small against the scale of what gets discarded — but it grew without advertising, which is unusual.

The foundation has also tried to sort out a problem the volunteers created themselves. Every session generates knowledge — which brands fail, which faults recur, which parts cannot be bought — and for years all of it stayed in people’s heads. In 2017, therefore, an online tool was launched so that groups could record what each repair turned out to involve. Moreover, the records made it possible to compare one town with another. In other words, a movement built on Saturday afternoons quietly began to carry out research.

Text B · What a Saturday actually looks like

Written for this course. The town described here is a composite of several such groups.

In practice, a session looks less impressive than the numbers. In one English town that started a group after a public meeting, nineteen people turned up on the first Saturday, most of them over sixty, and they repaired forty-one things before lunch. Nobody had to make up a reason for coming. A lamp is not a symbol of anything; it is a lamp, and it either works afterwards or it does not.

The economics are what persuade councils, however, rather than the sentiment. A repair typically costs a fraction of a replacement, and volunteers find out very quickly that a surprising share of dead appliances have one cheap broken part. Nevertheless, nobody pretends the saving is large in itself. Therefore the case for the shop tends to be financial before it is ever environmental. In that town the funding ran out in the second winter, and yet the group stayed open, staffed by eleven volunteers and one paid hour a week.

None of which has fixed the underlying problem. Manufacturers still design products that are difficult to open, and several countries are only now beginning to phase out the rules that allowed it. Even so, the interesting part of the story is not the tools or the money. What turned out to matter was that somebody organised an afternoon and other people came. That is the least repeatable part of it, and it is the only part the starter kit cannot explain, which is presumably why the foundation spends so much of its time answering the same question from towns that already have everything else they need.

steps.title: The patterns in one place
steps.html:
Lessons 33 and 34 together, plus what happens after a phrasal verb.

After a verb: some take -ing (admit, deny, avoid, finish, keep, suggest), some take the infinitive (decide, refuse, manage, hope, intend, agree), and six change meaning (remember, forget, stop, try, regret, go on).

After a preposition: always -ing. This includes the particle in many phrasal verbs: come up with solving it, fed up with waiting, the habit of stopping.

As a subject: -ing. Stopping early is the problem.

For purpose: the infinitive. They set up a website to test it.

The trap in this lesson: a phrasal verb ending in a preposition takes -ing, but one ending in an adverb particle can be followed by an infinitive. Compare They came up with testing it (with is a preposition) and They set out to test it (out is a particle, and the infinitive gives the purpose).

steps.title: Which form after a phrasal verb
steps.html:
1. Two phrasal verbs, two different answers.
  2. come up with ends in with, which is a preposition. Anything after it is a noun or an -ing form: They came up with testing it on students.
  3. set out ends in out, which is an adverb particle, not a preposition. It can be followed by an infinitive of purpose: They set out to test it on students.
  4. The test: can the particle take an object directly? with must (with something), so it is a preposition. out need not be, so it is a particle.
  5. In practice, learn the whole phrase. Look forward to, get round to, come up with, be used to all end in prepositions and all take -ing.

steps.placeholder: I was told for years that …
steps.html:
• Open with the belief and where you met it.
  • Turn on it with <i>However</i> or <i>Nevertheless</i>.
  • Concede something real with <i>Although</i>.
  • Restate with <i>In other words</i>.
  • Close with a result, using <i>Therefore</i>.

Useful language

  • Research carried out in … found out that …
  • However / Nevertheless, …
  • Although … , no study has ever turned up evidence that …
  • It turns out that …
  • In other words, …
  • Therefore the practical advice is …
steps.modelHtml:
The ten-minute rule

I was told for years that I was not a morning person, and I made decisions on that basis for most of my twenties. However, when I finally worked out where the belief came from, it turned out to be one comment made by a teacher in 1998.

The research that has been carried out on this is not flattering to anybody. Although people do differ genuinely in their body clocks, most of what we call a 'type' is a habit we have set up and then stopped questioning.

In other words, the label saves us the work of finding out what is actually true. Nevertheless, it survives, because it explains a real difficulty and costs nothing.

Therefore the dull advice: try the thing you have decided you cannot do, for ten minutes, before you rule it out.
